1:
The opening promise is heard as an answer to a division. Ellicott says the union of the ten tribes with the two is what fills the prophet's mind, that he cannot bear to think of a cleavage running through the religious and social life of the people being made permanent, and that this is the crown of the promise which closed the previous chapter: Israel should be Israel. Henry works the word families harder. It is not the two tribes only but all of them, not the house of Aaron and the families of Levi only but every family, and not the state at large only but particular households, from which he draws the note that the families of good people may apply to God in their family capacity and stay themselves on him. Gill reads the time-marker forward instead, to the days of the Gospel, when the Jews will weigh the old prophecies against what has happened and turn.

Clarke stands back and describes the chapter as a piece of staging. A distant scene opens with God expressing his regard and promising restoration; heralds then appear on Mount Ephraim proclaiming the arrival of the great jubilee and summoning the people to Zion; God resumes the speech with promises so gracious that the nations are called to attend; and then, by what Clarke calls a very happy invention, the mother of Joseph and Benjamin is raised from her tomb near Jerusalem to look about for her children and lament that none of them are in the land, before Ephraim in turn comes into view to bewail his own past errors.

Whose sword the survivors escaped is not agreed. Gill and Henry look back to the exodus, Gill naming the sword of Pharaoh at the sea, the Amalekites and Amorites, and even their own brethren after the calf and the affair at Baalpeor, and Henry making the whole verse a reminder of what God did for the fathers coming out of Egypt. Clarke takes it instead of the ten tribes who escaped the Assyrians, with the land of exile as the wilderness. Ellicott holds both ends at once: the captives who had escaped or would escape the sword of the Chaldeans, finding grace in the desert between Palestine and the Euphrates, and the more distant exiles beyond the Tigris as well. He adds the reason for reading it so, that the older deliverance had no such escape from a sword, which is why the language here is modified. What all of them agree on is Ellicott's underlying point, that a past experience of love is being offered as the pledge of a future one.

The clause about causing Israel to rest is difficult and they handle it differently. Ellicott says the verb takes in settling and establishing as well as giving rest, and would render it as an imperative in form, let me go to set him at rest. Calvin reports that interpreters agree in taking the infinitive as a past tense, notes that some refer it to God as the leader who brings his people to their rest, and prefers the simpler sense of Israel betaking himself to his own rest; he offers a version of his own and remarks how widely the early translations diverge here.

On the appearing from afar, Keil and Delitzsch have the prophet speaking in the name of the people and reckoning himself one of them. While Israel languished in exile the Lord had withdrawn and kept himself at a distance; now he is seen appearing again, and the distance is Zion, where he is enthroned and from which he sits to lead them home. They give the last verb its force as prolonging favour: because the love is everlasting, grace has been kept up toward them, which is the reason they were not destroyed.
3:
Who speaks in the clause about an appearance long ago, and whether the distance is in time at all, divides them at once. Gill canvasses three owners for the words: the prophet, the eternal Son, or the church acknowledging past mercies while complaining they are old and that God now hides his face; he notes the word saying is not in the text, which is what wrongly turns the sequel into more of her speech. Ellicott changes the axis: the Hebrew adverb points to distance rather than time, and a deliverer hears his people's cry from far off and draws near. Calvin hears something harsher, a clamour raised by unbelievers wanting a pretext for rejecting favour — God appeared to us, but it was long ago — which he says is how profane men still deride whatever God has testified in Law, Prophets or Gospel.

Clarke collects three renderings of the everlasting love — with the old love, with a love of long standing, and simply I love thee always — taking it of the love shown the fathers in Egypt, the desert and the land. He then argues against making the verse a decree of election, on the ground that few Jews since the return from Babylon have given evidence of being God's children; the words concern their state as a people, preserved by providence as a proof of the authority of the Scriptures. On the drawing that follows, Ellicott lists the competing versions, that God has respited them or continued his lovingkindness, and sides with the older translations. Calvin rejects the common rendering as frigid and unsuitable, reading instead a mercy not evanescent but following the people from year to year in every age.

The rebuilding is not of walls. Keil and Delitzsch take it for a permanent condition of increasing prosperity, the repeated verb confirming the promise, the virgin being the congregation entering a new and joyful phase. Ellicott says the building is more than towers and masonry, and makes the instrument a drum of the tambourine kind with bells on its hoop. Clarke explains the title virgin as marking a restoration to ancient purity, and notes such instruments were women's and belonged to rejoicing. Gill turns the figure to the church, espoused as a chaste virgin and built of living stones. Calvin uses the delay itself: seventy years might have extinguished faith, since when nothing appears but the bare word and God repeats the same promise daily we count it of no moment, measuring his power by our own and concluding that one who comes late will never come.

The vines bring in a piece of law, which four of them explain alike. For three years after planting the fruit was reckoned uncircumcised and might not be eaten, in the fourth it was holy to the Lord, and only in the fifth could the planter use it; to eat as common things is to enjoy one's own vintage undisturbed. Keil and Delitzsch add the contrast with planting for strangers who destroy the fruit; Calvin sets it against the old curse that another shall eat what you plant, taking the promise to imply how bare those rich mountains had been left. Wesley notes mountains suit vines, being open to the sun; Gill reads the planting of Gospel churches.

The watchmen divide them again. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott make them men posted on the hills to catch the first crescent after the new moon, so the festivals could be fixed, and Ellicott calls what follows all but decisive for that reading, the point being that the rival worship which had kept the ten tribes from the Temple was to cease. Clarke takes them for the prophets, calling both kingdoms to one worship. Calvin observes the prophet deliberately includes the ten tribes, and Wesley finds the fulfilment where the gospel was received in Galilee and Samaria.
7:
Who is told to sing is not settled. Gill takes it for the Gentile Christians called to rejoice over the conversion of the Jews, which will be to them as life from the dead, but reports a Jewish reading which shifts the words and makes it the Lord saying to Jacob, sing with gladness, as the old versions and the Targum do. Ellicott renders the next phrase over the head of the nations, meaning over Israel, a title another prophet suggests the ten tribes claimed, and has even the heathen called to rejoice in the restoration and pray for its prosperity, the verb for saving being the one that became the cry of Hosanna. Clarke agrees the chief of the nations is Jacob, this people having once been the most honourable on earth, and leaves the prayer open between the Jews interceding for their brethren and praising God for saving the remnant.

Calvin fixes the moment. The prophecy was given when the destruction of people, city and temple was close at hand, so the prophet was comforting the dead in their graves, to make them wait patiently and be sure that raising the dead is no harder for God than healing the sick.

The north is a technical direction. Calvin observes that whenever the prophets speak of deliverance they name the north, as when they threaten they say the army comes from the north, the earlier deliverance having come from the south because Egypt lay there. Gill takes it of Babylon at the seventy years' end, and then of the northern countries where the Jews are now numerous. Clarke divides the exiles, the ten tribes having been carried partly into Assyria and partly into Media, countries far enough off to be called in prophetic language the coasts of the earth. Ellicott makes the phrase wide enough for both Judah in Babylon and Israel in the cities of the Medes. Keil and Delitzsch give a reason for telling the remotest heathen: lest they imagine the God of Israel wanted power to save his own, and that they might learn to fear him.

The returning company is described by its weakest members. Ellicott notices that precisely those usually left behind as encumbrances are named, the blind, the lame, the woman with child and the woman in labour, concluding that none is to remain behind. Clarke makes it a promise of provision: difficulties removed, the journey supplied, bodies and minds so supported that the veriest invalids arrive.

Whether the weeping is grief or gladness is the sharpest split here. Gill offers both, tears of joy on two Jewish commentators' authority, or tears of repentance for their sins and above all for rejecting the Messiah. Clarke takes them as penitential only, men deeply deploring their sins while they beg for mercy. Ellicott will have all three, sorrow for the past, joy for the present and prayer for the future, with a partial fulfilment at the laying of the second foundation, where the old men wept while the rest shouted. Calvin rejects the joy reading and takes the verse adversatively: they went into exile weeping, and that is no impediment to their restoration. His model is the psalm of the sower, pressed hard, since exile was a sowing and the seed must die in the ground or stay barren. Wesley thinks the tense may be past rather than future, so that they went weeping, citing the same psalm, though allowing a weeping for joy as well as sorrow.

On the last clause Clarke says Ephraim, the most considerable tribe, commonly stands for the whole ten. Ellicott hears in firstborn an echo of what was said to Pharaoh, marking Ephraim for special favour now the birthright had passed from Reuben; Wesley reads the rivers of water against the older journey out of Egypt, through a wilderness where water often failed.
10:
Henry treats the summons as news. This is a work the nations cannot help noticing, so let them hear the prophecy in order to understand the performance, and pass it to the isles; it will spread the world over and look great in history, and we may see first how it looks in prophecy. He compresses the promise into an epigram, that the hand which gave the wound shall heal it: he who scattered knows where, and therefore where to find them. Ellicott makes the isles a vague representative of the distant west, and takes both nations and isles for heathen invited into Israel's praise. Calvin explains the lofty strain: seventy years is a whole lifetime, the people had been buried as in a grave, and the length of time alone was enough to cut off hope, so the prophet exclaims and despatches heralds everywhere.

On the two verbs for deliverance Ellicott distinguishes setting free from acting as the near kinsman, who was liberator and avenger both, and denies that the notion of a price paid lies in the Hebrew. Henry reaches the same conclusion by another route, that the redemption is by power and not by price, as of old out of Egypt. Gill widens the beneficiary from the patriarch and his natural posterity to all the elect of whatever nation; Wesley reads the deliverance and the entry into the land as types, of redemption by Christ and of the saints entering heaven. Calvin supplies the objection answered: the Chaldean monarchy looked like a gulf that had swallowed the world, and men comparing their case with any imaginable remedy would despair; but sheep in the jaws of wolves are not beyond rescue.

Calvin makes the height of Zion the point of the return. The promise is of the Temple restored, without which the journey home mattered little; if only quietness, wealth and pleasure were in question they had better have stayed, Chaldea being fertile and agreeable, and for the goods of this fading life the exile was the better place. What made returning worth doing was separation from the heathen and the right worship of God. Wesley identifies the height with the Temple, Henry recalls the singing when the foundation was laid, and Clarke makes the flowing together the gathering at the yearly feasts.

Three handle the watered garden devotionally. Clarke fills it with the light, life and power of God, so that they rejoice evermore and give thanks in everything; Henry says our souls are never worth calling gardens except as watered by the dews of the Spirit, and the promise about sorrow has no full accomplishment this side of the heavenly Zion. Wesley takes soul here for the whole man, and reads the gospel's joy and heaven's under the same words. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the picture, the redeemed streaming out from the sacred height and spreading over the country like water for the good things dealt out at home.

Two small points close it. Keil and Delitzsch observe the dancing belongs only to the virgins, the young men and old sharing the joy but not the figure. Calvin admits Israel danced while celebrating God's praises but insists it was chaste and a mode of worship, nothing like the wantonness the world indulges in when happy. On the priests, Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke agree the fatness is the fat of the thank-offerings, restored worship bringing them their share again; Calvin explains why they are singled out, as the heart of the people, the nation being incomplete without a priesthood, since without it they would have lived like heathen with no prescribed way of calling on God. Gill rejects the maintenance of ministers as too low a sense, offering either their being filled with the doctrine they must feed others with, or, the gospel knowing no separate order of priests, the whole body of the saints.
15:
Whether Ramah is a town at all is the first question. Gill notes the word means a high place, which is why the Targum paraphrases rather than transliterates. Ellicott presses further: the noun elsewhere carries the article when it is a proper name and here stands without one, so the sense may be simply from a mountain height, as the Latin version took it; if a place is meant it is probably the one in Benjamin. Clarke fixes on that town without hesitation, six or seven miles from Jerusalem, near which Rachel was buried. Wesley makes it the place where the Babylonian captain sorted the prisoners, releasing some, condemning others, sending the rest away, which caused the bitter weeping.

Calvin is more interested in the device than the geography. This is a personification, a woman long dead and reduced to ashes raised up to lament, and the discourse has more force that way than if the prophet had said the land would look waste and mournful. He notes the rhetoricians rank personification among the highest ornaments, and that a Roman authority on style held nothing moves an audience so much as raising the dead from below; the prophet, though never taught in their schools, adorns his speech in that very manner. Ellicott adds the structural point, that the contrast with the exulting joy just before shows a new section beginning, repeating in altered form the same pair of pictures, present woe and future gladness, with Rachel as mother of Joseph standing for the northern kingdom.

Whether the passage predicts the killing of the children at Bethlehem produces the flattest disagreement in the chapter. Clarke says the evangelist, ever fond of accommodation, applied the words because they suited the occasion, and states plainly they are not a prediction of that event; at the next verse he presses it, since those murdered infants never came again from the land of the enemy, whereas the exiles did. Wesley simply records that there was a lamentation like this one when the infants around Bethlehem were killed, and leaves the two side by side without adjudicating.

On the comfort offered, Gill allows sorrow of this kind may lawfully be indulged but holds it must be moderated, and that when relief comes from God himself the mournful voice is to stop and wet eyes to be dried. Calvin insists the point is not that grief is forbidden but that it will not be perpetual, since the exiles will return and the land that fell to Benjamin and Joseph will be inhabited again; the sorrow is to end happily and produce some benefit. Keil and Delitzsch keep the promise in the same terms, a reward for the work and a return from the enemy's land.

Ellicott works at what the work is. He traces the phrase to an older prophecy delivered to a king of Judah, and reads Rachel, personifying the northern kingdom or perhaps all Israel, as labouring at repentance and reformation with a mother's care, comforted that the labour will not be wasted. He states and sets aside the alternative, which refers the work instead to the travail of childbirth, as less satisfactory.

The last clause is read forward. Ellicott improves it to hope for thy future, notes the same words elsewhere rendered an expected end, and defines the hope as the return of the ten tribes from captivity. Gill takes the posterity sense and pushes it further, to the children who had been massacred rising again to a blessed immortality. Calvin uses the word end to establish the shape of the oracle: had their happiness run in one unbroken stream the word would not suit, since it names a termination, so a contrast is intended between the end and the beginning, and the grievous time meanwhile is to be borne patiently.
18:
Ephraim here is a people speaking as one man. Gill takes the name for Israel, the ten tribes and even the whole nation, and reads the passage of their conversion in a later day, granting the patriarch himself, a tender-hearted man, could be introduced as Rachel just was. Henry says the singular marks unanimity, so they should be as one man in repenting, and also fits the words to particular penitents; he too recalls the man of that name mourning for his children many days. Ellicott keeps the northern exiles in view: longest under the discipline of suffering, they must by now, the prophet reckons, have learnt repentance, and in it, treated as accomplished, he finds fresh ground of hope for Judah.

The bullock is explained alike by all who touch it. Wesley notes such beasts are unruly when first yoked; Clarke has the speaker confess he was an unbroken and untoward steer who rebelled the more he was chastised and has profited only now; Ellicott calls it the nearest thing in the older Scriptures to the Greek proverb about kicking against the goads. Henry allows two senses to the admission of being chastised: either that it was well he was, since otherwise he had been undone; or that it records a want of feeling, the chastisement being all there was, nothing awakened by it and nothing looked for beyond.

On the prayer to be turned they converge. Clarke has a man willing at last to take the yoke and finding he has no power, able only to will and pray, so he asks God to take the matter into his own hand. Henry hears the same helplessness, a man bent to backslide who cannot keep close to God, still less bring himself back, whose petition implies that unless grace turns him he will wander endlessly; but God works with power and makes the unwilling willing. Calvin puts it doctrinally: a sinner's repenting is God's peculiar work and cannot be ascribed to human strength.

The order of the two experiences then divides them. Gill puts conversion first and repentance after: the prayer was answered, and only then came repentance, not of gross actions only but of inward corruptions and even of sins in holy things, which is evangelical repentance and cannot precede a real turning. Clarke orders it differently, making conviction first, since as soon as a man sees himself lost he is convicted, and contrition follows conviction. Ellicott reports a commentator who refers the turning back to the apostasy rather than forward to repentance, and rejects it, the word repeating the one used a verse before and being more naturally a penitent's first motion.

The gesture of grief takes two of them outside the text. Clarke says smiting the thigh was a usual sign of deep affliction and the same among the ancient Greeks, quotes two passages of Homer with an English poet's rendering, and adds he has often seen people in deep grief do it. Ellicott ranges it with the publican's smiting on his breast as an Eastern expression of extremest grief, and quotes the same poet for the gesture. Henry keeps it moral rather than antiquarian: the man is amazed at his own stupidity, ashamed and confounded, unable to look up to God with confidence.

The last clause looks back further than the exile. Henry observes that finding one sin should set us searching for more, and that the sin of our youth was its reproach and should often be remembered against ourselves in penitential shame. Wesley makes it the just punishment of sins long committed. Calvin closes on the use of it: we shun whatever is hard to the flesh, so we must regard the end, and when we see God had our salvation in view while handling us roughly the sorrow is lessened, since had he indulged them their pride would only have grown.
20:
Whether the opening question expects yes or no splits them. Gill grants a question in this Hebrew form usually denies the more vehemently, which would make Ephraim no dear son, but says that runs against the scope of the passage, and renders it is not Ephraim my dear son, to which the answer is yes. Ellicott sets out both: affirmatively the words are a father's yearning over a son still loved, God wondering at his own affection for so rebellious a creature; negatively they press the faults as destroying all claim to love. He judges the affirmative far the better, since every word of reproof or invitation here carries a loving remembrance. Calvin takes the other side. A question makes a thing stronger, since the asker shows what he asks is too plain to be denied; the sense is that Ephraim was unworthy of honour and no object of delight, having annihilated the favour of his adoption so far as he could.

On the next clause Ellicott corrects the version: the preposition can hardly mean against, for which this prophet uses other words, the sense being rather as often as I speak to him. Wesley keeps the received reading, drawing from it that since the threatenings God has remembered him with a father's compassion.

The waymarks are travellers' cairns. Clarke has heaps of stones such as men set up in the desert to find the way back, and puts it bluntly: mark the road to Babylon, for thither you shall go and from it as certainly return. Wesley agrees they must mind the way their captors take. Ellicott notices the figure changing, from Ephraim the dear son to Israel the backsliding daughter, and has the first returning party set the marks up for those who follow, so the road walked in shame is walked again in joy, through the cities that saw it. Calvin explains why the instruction was needed: men carried into Chaldea assumed the way back closed and lived among foreigners as though dead to the land, knowing they had forfeited it and not believing the punishment temporary.

The reproach that follows is read as restlessness. Ellicott makes it the pacing to and fro of impatient desire, the penitent but still adulterous wife hesitating between her lovers and her husband, as in another prophet's parable. Calvin gives the verb its literal force of going round, and calls circuits the crooked speculations the unbelieving weary themselves with. Gill takes it geographically, of wandering from country to country as the Jews still do, and notes the word carries the sense of folly in Arabic.

Then comes the hardest clause in the chapter, and two go out of their way to reject the familiar reading. Ellicott fixes the translators' sense by a line of Shakespeare, where to compass is to woo and win, and finds the point in an inversion: the bridegroom woos, but here the erring wife shall woo her divine husband. He lists and dismisses the alternatives, that a woman shall be turned into a man, or protect one, or put one to flight; and says the connection with the Incarnation belongs to dreams rather than realities, lacking even an allusion in the New Testament and excluded by the word used for woman. Clarke is equally sure no such meaning is in the words or context, mentions an emendation in two manuscripts giving the wife shall return to her husband, doubts that would be called a new thing, and prefers a weak people overcoming the strong man who had oppressed them. Wesley reads it of the church, small in numbers against many and powerful enemies, prevailing all the same. Henry holds the position the other two are refusing: the new and extraordinary thing is a creation, a work of almighty power, the human nature of Christ formed by the Holy Ghost, set here to encourage the exiles home.
23:
Ellicott turns the eye from the northern kingdom to Judah, which shares the restoration, once more a faithful city with righteousness in it, the holy mountain naming the Temple hill. On the husbandmen and shepherds he draws an ideal: a people pastoral without being nomadic, agricultural yet sharing the culture and safety of cities, in sharp contrast to the ruined fields and empty pastures round the prophet. Wesley notes the two divine titles prefacing these promises, one asserting power to do the thing and the other the goodness that means it. Calvin adds that the promise reaches the villages too, since cities are often full while the fields lie empty for fear of an enemy.

Calvin disputes the rendering of the satisfied soul. The word is commonly given as weary, but he takes it for thirsty, citing a psalm where a soul is like dry land, since weariness cannot properly be said of land, and noting the paired verb means to water or satiate; weariness and thirst go together, which is how one word serves for both. Gill keeps the weariness and applies it to sinners at their first awakening, labouring after a righteousness they cannot find till they come to Christ; the verb, he notes, means not to satisfy only but to inebriate. Ellicott hears an anticipation of the thought and almost the language of the Gospel, the hungry filled and the weary given rest.

Whose sleep was sweet is disputed. Gill and Clarke agree the oracle had been delivered in a dream, from which the prophet woke at the last words; Clarke passes on another suggestion, that the words are a wish, a prophet who cannot live to see such days asking to wake from his tomb, content to go back once he had. Keil and Delitzsch report expositors who refer the waking to God, since God speaks in the context and the psalms sometimes call on him to awake, and answer that a man may say his sleep was sweet but God may not. Ellicott lists two further readings, one making it the husband who dreamt of his wife's return, another a psalm quotation about freedom from dark dreams, and finds the prophet's own words far more natural. Calvin explains it from the opposite feeling: considering these terrible judgments the prophet had been as though overwhelmed with sleep, in which, as in darkness, men cannot tell black from white.

Henry has him going back to sleep on purpose, hoping for more, and not disappointed. Ellicott makes the next promise turn on the prophet's own call, some twenty-three years earlier: the almond, the wakeful or watching tree, with the play on its name, and the verbs of his commission all return, but the work that was mostly rooting out and pulling down is now the happier one of building and planting. Calvin supplies the objection answered, that a God who allowed the ruin might have prevented it, and replies that the hand which chastised can relieve whenever it pleases.

On the sour grape, Keil and Delitzsch reject the reading which makes the fathers begin eating before the children's teeth were blunted, since the tenses set the blunting down as a result of the eating; the saying means children atone for their fathers' misdeeds. Clarke gives the same sense and correction, that no child suffers divine punishment for a father's sin except so far as he acts the same way himself. Calvin notes another prophet quotes the same complaint, and finds a pagan poet telling his countrymen that the Roman undeservedly pays for his fathers' faults; the proverb will die out, he says, because men tamed by their evils will see at last that God had not dealt severely without cause. Gill takes it forward: after the captivity no public calamity would fall for the fathers' sins and their own together, but for their own alone.
31:
Ellicott asks his readers to feel how bold the announcement is. Familiarity hides it, but a covenant delivered with every conceivable sanction as from God is here set aside as a man repeals an earthly law, and whoever could say that without trembling must have been sure he was himself taught of God and that the new teaching stood higher. He traces what came of the phrase: the words used at the last supper, the argument of the letter to the Hebrews, the doctrine of justification by faith, and the titles by which the two collections of Scripture are still known.

What makes it new is disputed in detail. Keil and Delitzsch define the term, since to cut a covenant is not to make an appointment but to establish mutual obligations, God bestowing his favours and men bound to the commands laid on them; they refuse to fix the day of the taking by the hand either to the departure from Egypt or the ceremony at Sinai, referring it to the whole exodus, which ended only at the entry into the land. Wesley denies the covenant is new in substance, since it was made with Abraham and with the people afterwards; it is new in being revealed after a new manner, more fully and plainly, in excluding the ceremonial law, and in the far greater efficacy of the Spirit attending it. Gill locates the newness elsewhere: the Sinai covenant was not properly one of works but typical, faulty in some sense or at least kept by faulty persons, and made with Israelites only, where this belongs to Jews and Gentiles alike.

Calvin makes the passage turn on a comparison. The promise is not of the dignity they had lost but of something better, and since the law was a rule of the most perfect doctrine, nothing superior could be hoped for without Christ; take Christ away and we must remain in the law. He keeps the contrast sharp because no Jew thought God could add anything better to the law, and those who valued it least were loudest that heaven and earth would sooner mix than any change be made in it, while they clung to what God had instituted only for a time.

On what the difference actually is they converge. Keil and Delitzsch set the phrase for putting the law within them against the standing expression for setting it before them, and writing on the heart against writing on tables of stone. Ellicott says the experiment of a law requiring righteousness had been tried and failed, and what remained was the hope, now turned into assurance, of a power imparting righteousness, written in the inward parts where God requires truth. Clarke fixes the time as the sealing of vision and prophecy, the assuming of the body prepared, the laying down of the life and the ascension by which the Spirit's gift was obtained. Wesley states the distinction flatly: the first shows duty, the second brings the grace of regeneration by which the heart is changed and enabled for duty.

Calvin raises the obvious objection against himself, and Wesley reaches the same answer. Was the grace of regeneration wanting to the fathers under the law? Calvin calls the suggestion preposterous. Those who were regenerated then obtained the favour through Christ, so that it was transferred to them, as it were, from another source; the power of penetrating the heart was never inherent in the law but was lent to it by the Gospel. What he concedes is that the grace was rare and little known under the law and has been poured out more abundantly since. Wesley says the same in his own words: all under the law who came to salvation were saved by this new covenant, but it was not then evidently exhibited, and regenerating grace was not so common as it has since become.
34:
The promise that no one will need teaching has to be defended against a use nobody here accepts. Calvin says fanatics have ignorantly abused the passage to put down teaching altogether, and answers that the words are hyperbole in the service of a comparison. It is not said simply that no man shall teach his neighbour, but that no man shall need to say know the Lord, and that phrase names the first elements of the faith; the promise is that God's people will no longer be alphabetarians, kept in the rudiments as the ancient people were kept, since the least of the faithful now sees more clearly what belongs to salvation than the most learned did then. Gill defends the ministry on the same side. The words cannot mean the outward preaching of the word, which will be needless only in the New Jerusalem and is needed in every period before it; nor do they forbid brotherly instruction or Christian conversation. What they exclude is the private man's pretended revelation and the magisterial dictate of a man in office, the written word being the only rule; or else the saying is comparative and not absolute.

Calvin then sets the verse against another prophet who seems to say the opposite, that each man shall take his neighbour by the hand and call him to go up and be taught. His reconciliation is that the two describe different things: one denies that the people will still need first principles, the other has them helping each other on to the knowledge of God's law. He adds a caution against pressing the promise too far in another direction, since the knowledge is not said to be equal in all, experience proving otherwise and the measure of God's gifts being according to his own pleasure.

Ellicott reads the verse out of a mood rather than a doctrine. Behind it lies the profound sense of failure that oppressed this prophet as it has oppressed many true teachers since: what had come of all the machinery of ritual and instruction the law had provided so abundantly? The repeated exhortations of preachers to know the Lord had become a dreary monotony, like an old worm-eaten homily. To know him as he is would take nothing less than a revelation of his presence to each man's own heart, and that is what is here promised to whoever will receive it.

Clarke turns the promise into a report on his own century. It is to be a time of universal light, when all shall know God from the least to the greatest and children shall be taught to read the new covenant and understand the terms of their salvation; and it is to be a time of general pardon, with multitudes daily receiving the witness of the Spirit and confessing it in their lives. Then he names what he thinks the fulfilment: how wonderfully, he says, is this prophecy fulfilled in the age of Bibles, of Sunday schools and of village preaching.

The last clause is where Ellicott is most careful. The promise to remember sin no more repeats the promise to forgive, but does it after the manner of men, since our thought of God as knowing everything rules out any limit on his knowledge such as forgetting would imply. What is meant is that he will be to the man who repents and knows him as men are to men when they forget and forgive: the past offences will be treated as though they had never happened, so far as they touch the soul's communion with him, however their consequences may run on. Wesley puts the same clause at the root of everything else in the passage, making the free pardon and remission of sins the thing all the rest of this grace grows from.
35:
Henry treats these verses as the ratification of everything promised before. Glorious things have been said, but may they be depended on? What is secured here is that while the world stands God will have a church in it, which may be brought very low and will be raised again; and two things are offered to confirm it, the building of the world and the rebuilding of Jerusalem. He who built all things at first is the same who makes all things now, so the constancy of the kingdom of nature may encourage us to trust the promise for the continuance of the kingdom of grace.

Calvin explains why so much weight had to be put on the argument. It was hard to believe a people would not merely recover what they had lost but be made happier than before, when the church was in a state of complete despondency; and even a church raised a hundred times from the dead might be crushed a hundred times again, since grievous evils were still ahead of it. That is why the prophet dwells at such length on proving one thing.

The way the heavens are described draws a remarkable comment from Calvin. God is made to speak of the daily circuit of the sun and moon, and Calvin says the prophets spoke popularly and according to common notions: had they philosophised as the astronomers do, and spoken of the monthly course of the moon and the yearly course of the sun, the common people could not have followed them. They were content to state what even children could take in. Gill keeps to the plain sense of the ordinances, that the lights should leave their proper course, fail of their functions, desert their master or disobey his orders; and Wesley defines them as the establishments by which God works natural causes in their order.

Clarke turns the comparison into a claim about his own day. As surely as the sun gives light by day, he says, so surely will this people continue distinct from every other; and he holds the prophecy has been literally fulfilled so far, since every attempt in any country to naturalise them and merge them with its population has come to nothing. He names the most recent instance, an effort made in his own country in the year he was writing and supported, he says, by the strongest public interest, which had failed like the rest; and he refers the failure to the purpose declared in these very verses.

The last comparison changes the ground from constancy to measurement. Ellicott says the thought of the previous verse returns with a modification, since besides the stability of nature standing as a parable of the steadfastness of God's purposes there is now implied a sense that a finite mind can no more fathom how he works those purposes out than it can measure what to the prophet was an illimitable heaven and an unsearchable earth. Calvin reads it as the impossibility of God forgetting his covenant. Exile might have looked like a permanent death and made the truth of God come to nothing, and though a condition was attached to the covenant it never rested on the integrity of men, so that God is not a liar though every one of them proved faithless. Setting impossible things before us is his way of making us know he will at last be reconciled to a people he has justly punished. Gill takes the measuring literally enough to name what could not be measured, either the distance between the highest heavens and the earth or the extent of the heavens from one end to the other; and Calvin adds that none of this could comfort a hypocrite, since the promise is not addressed to men who have no intention of returning.
38:
Ellicott admits the drop feels like an anti-climax, from the loftiest promises in the book to a list of obscure landmarks, but explains it by how vividly the restored city stood before the prophet's mind, as before an earlier prophet's and, on a far larger scale, a later one. He saw a goodly city rising from the ruins, consecrated in fact and not in name, and described what made it different.

Whether the city meant is the one actually rebuilt divides them. Clarke says it cannot be, for two reasons: this one is much greater in extent, and permanent, never to be thrown down; so if the words are literal at all they mean a city built at some later ingathering. Gill reports a rabbi saying the same, that the prophecy belongs to a later redemption and was never fulfilled under the second temple, and takes the rebuilding himself as a figure of the church, holiness and perpetuity being ascribed to it. Calvin keeps the historical city and holds the point is that its extent and splendour after the return would not fall short of what they were under David; he compares a later prophet making the same promise to a people whose restored city at first fell far short of the old.

They divide again on its size. Calvin reports that most interpreters take the measuring line going forth to mean enlargement beyond the old walls, and declines it: the other prophet promises the city shall be inhabited in its own place, so the comparison is between ancient greatness and greatness to come, not a smaller circuit and a larger. Wesley agrees, taking it built round about on its old foundations. Clarke goes the other way, noting the two hills named lay outside the old limits and are destined to fall within the new.

Gill stops at a word read but not written, the vowel points standing where letters do not, and makes an argument of it: those who deny the antiquity of the pointing should consider it, the Jews never having suffered anything added to their Bible.

The place-names defeat them differently. Calvin declines them outright, saying he can tell us little because the ancient situation of the city is unknown, and that those who conjecture about such things only display their ignorance. Ellicott notes neither name occurs elsewhere, so any position is guesswork; he derives the first from the word for a leper, setting it outside the walls where such sufferers lived, and offers a northern hill named by the historian of the war. The second he calls of doubtful etymology, reporting a scholar who makes it high-towering, for the height above the Kidron later crowned by a fortress. Clarke identifies the second name with Golgotha, the heap of Gotha, which as the place of the crucifixion lay outside the city.

On the valley the names themselves are read as memorials. Keil and Delitzsch take it for the valley of Hinnom, the word covering carcases of beasts and of men left unburied after a judgment, and connect the name with its pollution under Josiah. Calvin takes the ashes for those swept from the altar after the sacrifices were burnt, and says the other name was given because a host of enemies had been destroyed there in Hezekiah's day, so the mercy might stay known to later generations, as Wesley does. Ellicott makes us look as the prophet did during the siege: the valley filled with corpses lying in the streets, the ashes of burnt houses choking them with rubble, the open ground running to the Kidron, a scene of unspeakable desolation which he sees in vision cleansed and as holy as the Temple precincts. Clarke ends with a Latin line bidding the happy times make speed; Wesley reads the perpetuity as belonging to the church, against which the gates of hell shall not prevail.
